claim: The TP53 tumor-suppressor gene is mutated in >50% of human tumors.
source: The TP53 tumor-suppressor gene is mutated in >50% of human tumors and Li-Fraumeni patients with germ line inactivation are predisposed to developing cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Li-Fraumeni patients with germ line TP53 inactivation are predisposed to developing cancer.
source: The TP53 tumor-suppressor gene is mutated in >50% of human tumors and Li-Fraumeni patients with germ line inactivation are predisposed to developing cancer.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the literature, cited in the introduction.

claim: tp53 deleted zebrafish spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors.
source: Here, we generated tp53 deleted zebrafish that spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia for which no animal model has been developed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by histological data and images in Figure 1.

claim: tp53 deleted zebrafish spontaneously develop angiosarcomas.
source: Here, we generated tp53 deleted zebrafish that spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia for which no animal model has been developed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by histological data and images in Figure 1.

claim: tp53 deleted zebrafish spontaneously develop germ cell tumors.
source: Here, we generated tp53 deleted zebrafish that spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia for which no animal model has been developed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by histological data and images in Figure 1.

claim: tp53 deleted zebrafish spontaneously develop an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia.
source: Here, we generated tp53 deleted zebrafish that spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia for which no animal model has been developed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by histological data, RNA sequencing, and images in Figures 1-3.

claim: No animal model has been developed for aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia prior to this study.
source: Here, we generated tp53 deleted zebrafish that spontaneously develop malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive Natural Killer cell-like leukemia for which no animal model has been developed.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The tp53 deletion was generated in syngeneic zebrafish.
source: Because the tp53 deletion was generated in syngeneic zebrafish, engraftment of fluorescent-labeled tumors could be dynamically visualized over time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and methods, describing the use of CG1 strain zebrafish.

claim: Engraftment of fluorescent-labeled tumors could be dynamically visualized over time in tp53 deleted zebrafish.
source: Because the tp53 deletion was generated in syngeneic zebrafish, engraftment of fluorescent-labeled tumors could be dynamically visualized over time.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and Figure 4 with whole animal imaging.

claim: Engrafted tumors shared gene expression signatures with predicted cells of origin in human tissue.
source: Importantly, engrafted tumors shared gene expression signatures with predicted cells of origin in human tissue.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: tp53del/del enhanced invasion and metastasis in kRASG12D-induced embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS).
source: Finally, we showed that tp53del/del enhanced invasion and metastasis in kRASG12D-induced embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), but did not alter the overall frequency of cancer stem cells, suggesting novel pro-metastatic roles for TP53 loss-of-function in human muscle tumors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation experiments and imaging in Figure 4, with statistical analysis showing p=0.003.

claim: tp53del/del did not alter the overall frequency of cancer stem cells in ERMS.
source: Finally, we showed that tp53del/del enhanced invasion and metastasis in kRASG12D-induced embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), but did not alter the overall frequency of cancer stem cells, suggesting novel pro-metastatic roles for TP53 loss-of-function in human muscle tumors.
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution transplantation assays shown in Table 1, with p=0.647.

claim: TP53 loss-of-function has novel pro-metastatic roles in human muscle tumors.
source: Finally, we showed that tp53del/del enhanced invasion and metastasis in kRASG12D-induced embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), but did not alter the overall frequency of cancer stem cells, suggesting novel pro-metastatic roles for TP53 loss-of-function in human muscle tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing increased metastasis without changes in stem cell frequency.

claim: TP53 is commonly inactivated by single amino acid mutations that create dominant-negative forms of the protein.
source: TP53 is commonly inactivated by single amino acid mutations that create dominant-negative forms of the protein that inhibit efficient tetramer formation and block transcriptional activity (Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller and Vousden, 2014.

claim: Dominant-negative TP53 mutations inhibit efficient tetramer formation and block transcriptional activity.
source: TP53 is commonly inactivated by single amino acid mutations that create dominant-negative forms of the protein that inhibit efficient tetramer formation and block transcriptional activity (Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller and Vousden, 2014.

claim: TP53 alleles likely alter transcriptional activity of TP53 and its related transcription factor family members, TP63 and TP73.
source: In this setting, TP53 alleles likely alter transcriptional activity of TP53 and its related transcription factor family members, TP63 and TP73 (Lang et al., 2004; Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lang et al., 2004 and Olive et al., 2004.

claim: TP53 deletion is expected to have less wide-ranging transcriptional effects that are confined to tetrameric transcription factor function.
source: By contrast, TP53 deletion is expected to have less wide-ranging transcriptional effects that are confined to tetrameric transcription factor function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement comparing deletion to point mutations.

claim: TP53 transcriptional inactivation can lead to genomic instability and impaired apoptotic responses.
source: Regardless of the genetic alteration, TP53 transcriptional inactivation can lead to genomic instability and impaired apoptotic responses that often are predisposing to a wide array of cancers (Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017 and Muller and Vousden, 2014.

claim: Several murine genetic models have been developed to assess the effects of both loss- and gain-of-function Tp53 mutations in cancer.
source: To date, several murine genetic models have been developed to assess the effects of both loss- and gain-of-function Tp53 mutations in cancer (Donehower et al., 1992; Harvey et al., 1993; Jacks et al., 1994; Lang et al., 2004; Lavigueur et al., 1989; Lee et al., 1994; Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to mouse model studies.

claim: Both Tp53 mutant and null alleles spontaneously develop cancer in mice.
source: Both Tp53 mutant and null alleles spontaneously develop cancer.
evidence: This is stated based on previous mouse model studies.

claim: The spectrum of tumors varies among different Tp53 alleles in mice.
source: However, similar to human Li-Fraumeni patients, the spectrum varies among different alleles, suggesting that the mode of Tp53 inactivation has important implications in regulating the types of cancer that develop, the time to onset, and the overall propensity for tumor progression (Lavigueur et al., 1989; Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lavigueur et al., 1989 and Lee et al., 1994.

claim: Mice heterozygous for the 172His point mutation are predisposed to developing osteosarcoma.
source: For example, mice heterozygous for the 172His point mutation are predisposed to developing osteosarcoma while animals harboring the 270His mutation develop hemangiosarcoma and carcinoma (Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olive et al., 2004.

claim: Mice harboring the 270His mutation develop hemangiosarcoma and carcinoma.
source: For example, mice heterozygous for the 172His point mutation are predisposed to developing osteosarcoma while animals harboring the 270His mutation develop hemangiosarcoma and carcinoma (Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olive et al., 2004.

claim: Mice with homozygous Tp53 deletion mainly develop lymphoma.
source: By contrast, mice with homozygous Tp53 deletion mainly develop lymphoma, with rare cases of angiosarcoma, undifferentiated sarcoma, osteosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, testicular tumors, nervous system tumors, teratoma, and mammary carcinoma being reported (Donehower et al., 1992; Harvey et al., 1993; Jacks et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Donehower et al., 1992; Harvey et al., 1993; Jacks et al., 1994.

claim: A small subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome patients harbor genomic deletions in the TP53 locus.
source: Importantly, a small subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome patients harbor genomic deletions in the TP53 locus and cancers that develop in dominant-negative, heterozygous point-mutation carriers often display deletion of the second TP53 allele (Malkin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malkin, 2011.

claim: Cancers that develop in dominant-negative, heterozygous TP53 point-mutation carriers often display deletion of the second TP53 allele.
source: Importantly, a small subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome patients harbor genomic deletions in the TP53 locus and cancers that develop in dominant-negative, heterozygous point-mutation carriers often display deletion of the second TP53 allele (Malkin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malkin, 2011.

claim: TP53 is commonly mutated in human sarcomas and is predictive of poor outcome.
source: TP53 is also commonly mutated in human sarcomas and is predictive of poor outcome (Taubert et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taubert et al., 1996.

claim: The TP53 locus is mutated in 16% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS).
source: For example, the TP53 locus is mutated in 16% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), a common pediatric cancer of muscle and transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of human ERMS through TP53 locus disruption or MDM2 amplification (Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2000.

claim: Transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of human ERMS through TP53 locus disruption or MDM2 amplification.
source: For example, the TP53 locus is mutated in 16% of human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), a common pediatric cancer of muscle and transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of human ERMS through TP53 locus disruption or MDM2 amplification (Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2000.

claim: TP53 mutations are acquired at ERMS relapse.
source: Interestingly, TP53 mutations are also acquired at ERMS relapse (Chen et al., 2013), suggesting a likely role for TP53 in ERMS progression and therapy resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: TP53 has a likely role in ERMS progression and therapy resistance.
source: Interestingly, TP53 mutations are also acquired at ERMS relapse (Chen et al., 2013), suggesting a likely role for TP53 in ERMS progression and therapy resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TP53 mutations are acquired at relapse.

claim: Li-Fraumeni patients with germline TP53 mutations commonly develop ERMS.
source: Finally, Li-Fraumeni patients with germline TP53 mutations commonly develop ERMS (Malkin, 2011), suggesting important roles for TP53 loss in the genesis of this disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malkin, 2011.

claim: Genetically engineered mouse and human xenograft models of ERMS do not metastasize in vivo.
source: Moreover, because genetically engineered mouse and human xenograft models of ERMS do not metastasize in vivo, assessing TP53 loss-of-function in the context of rhabdomyosarcoma metastasis has not been possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models.

claim: No tp53 deletion models have been generated in syngeneic zebrafish prior to this study.
source: Finally, to date, no tp53 deletion models have been generated in syngeneic zebrafish, precluding large-scale transplantation studies to assess how deletion regulates cancer stem cells and tumor invasion in vivo for a wide array of cancers.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field that this study addresses.

claim: A complete loss-of-function tp53 deletion allele was generated in syngeneic CG1-strain zebrafish using TALEN endonucleases.
source: To better study tp53 biology in vivo, we generated a complete loss-of-function tp53 deletion allele in syngeneic CG1-strain zebrafish using TALEN endonucleases.
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The tp53del/del model contrasts with currently available point-mutation alleles for zebrafish tp53 that predominantly develop MPNSTs.
source: This model contrasts with currently available point-mutation alleles for zebrafish tp53 that predominantly develop MPNSTs (Berghmans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berghmans et al., 2005 and comparison of tumor spectra.

claim: tp53del/del tumors efficiently transplanted into recipient fish.
source: Moreover, because the tp53del/del mutant was generated in CG1-strain syngeneic zebrafish (Mizgireuv and Revskoy, 2006), tumors efficiently transplanted into recipient fish enabling expansion of unlabeled and GFP-labeled tumors, dynamic live animal imaging of metastatic progression, and analysis of transcriptional differences between tumors using RNA sequencing approaches.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 with high engraftment rates.

claim: The overall frequency of ERMS self-renewing cancer stem cells was unaffected by loss of tp53.
source: Using these approaches, we showed that the overall frequency of ERMS self-renewing cancer stem cells was unaffected by loss of tp53.
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assays in Table 1 showing p=0.647.

claim: tp53del/del ERMS were more invasive than tp53wt/wt ERMS.
source: In contrast, tp53del/del ERMS were more invasive, providing a potential explanation for increased aggression associated with TP53 disruption in human ERMS (Seki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation experiments in Figure 4 showing p=0.003.

claim: A 12.1 kb tp53 genomic sequence was deleted in the CG1 tp53del/del allele.
source: F1 embryos were screened by genomic PCR to identify a single founder line with deletion of 12.1 kb tp53 genomic sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the methods.

claim: Homozygous tp53del/del embryos lacked Tp53 protein expression.
source: As expected, homozygous tp53del/del embryos lacked protein expression and were resistant to radiation-induced apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Homozygous tp53del/del embryos were resistant to radiation-induced apoptosis.
source: As expected, homozygous tp53del/del embryos lacked protein expression and were resistant to radiation-induced apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown by TUNEL staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D with p<0.001.

claim: Both heterozygous tp53wt/del and homozygous tp53del/del fish survived until adulthood at expected ratios.
source: Progeny from tp53wt/del crosses were also raised to adulthood and assessed for viability and tumor onset over time. Both heterozygous tp53 wt/del and homozygous tp53del/del fish survived until adulthood at expected ratios (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with survival curves.

claim: By 4 months of age, tp53del/del zebrafish began to spontaneously develop tumors.
source: By 4 months of age, tp53del/del zebrafish began to spontaneously develop tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Phenotypes of the earliest malignant tp53del/del cohort were consistent with loss of osmoregulation and kidney damage.
source: Phenotypes of the earliest malignant tp53del/del cohort were consistent with loss of osmoregulation and kidney damage.
evidence: This is stated based on observation of the animals.

claim: Histopathological analysis of early malignant tp53del/del animals revealed features consistent with leukemia.
source: Histopathological analysis of these animals revealed features consistent with leukemia, including blast-like cells predominating in the kidney marrow and loss of kidney stromal architecture, including effacement of the renal tubules (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B-D with histology images.

claim: Beginning by 7 months of age, a subset of tp53del/del animals developed externally visible tumors.
source: Beginning by 7 months of age, a subset of tp53del/del animals developed externally visible tumors and histology consistent with angiosarcoma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) (Figure 1E–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Berghmans et al., 2005; Choorapoikayil et al., 2012; Parant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: MPNST assignment was validated using IHC staining for sox10.
source: MPNST assignment was validated using IHC staining for sox10, which is a well-established clinical marker for this tumor type (Figure 1J) (Shin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J with sox10 immunohistochemistry.

claim: sox10 is a well-established clinical marker for MPNST.
source: MPNST assignment was validated using IHC staining for sox10, which is a well-established clinical marker for this tumor type (Figure 1J) (Shin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shin et al., 2012.

claim: tp53wt/del zebrafish infrequently developed tumors.
source: As expected, tp53wt/del zebrafish infrequently developed tumors, which is consistent with studies in other tp53 deficiency mouse models (Donehower et al., 1992; Harvey et al., 1993; Jacks et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to mouse model studies.

claim: 37% of tp53del/del animals developed externally visible tumors by 12 months of age.
source: In total, 37% of tp53del/del animals developed externally visible tumors by 12 months of age with a wider tumor spectrum than previously reported in homozygous tp53M214K and tp53I166T mutant zebrafish (Figure 1N,O) (Berghmans et al., 2005; Parant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1N with a survival curve.

claim: tp53del/del zebrafish have a wider tumor spectrum than previously reported in homozygous tp53M214K and tp53I166T mutant zebrafish.
source: In total, 37% of tp53del/del animals developed externally visible tumors by 12 months of age with a wider tumor spectrum than previously reported in homozygous tp53M214K and tp53I166T mutant zebrafish (Figure 1N,O) (Berghmans et al., 2005; Parant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited studies and shown in Figure 1O.

claim: tp53M214K and tp53I166T point mutation models predominantly developed MPNSTs.
source: For example, these point mutation models predominantly developed MPNSTs with only a rare, single melanoma being detected in homozygous animals (Berghmans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berghmans et al., 2005.

claim: The spectrum in tp53del/del zebrafish was more similar to that reported in Tp53-null mice than to tp53 point mutation zebrafish.
source: Remarkably, the spectrum in tp53del/del zebrafish was more similar to that reported in Tp53-null mice, with angiosarcomas and germ cell tumors occurring in both models (Donehower et al., 1992; Harvey et al., 1993; Jacks et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with mouse model literature.

claim: The predominance of T cell lymphomas seen in Tp53-null mice was not observed in tp53del/del zebrafish.
source: However, the predominance of T cell lymphomas seen in Tp53-null mice was not observed in tp53del/del zebrafish, likely reflecting species differences in sensitivity to Tp53 loss in target cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and interpreted as species differences.

claim: Species differences in sensitivity to Tp53 loss in target cells likely explain the lack of T cell lymphomas in tp53del/del zebrafish.
source: However, the predominance of T cell lymphomas seen in Tp53-null mice was not observed in tp53del/del zebrafish, likely reflecting species differences in sensitivity to Tp53 loss in target cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed differences.

claim: Primary MPNSTs that arose in the eye were orthotopically transplanted into the equivalent periocular space or into the peritoneum of CG1-strain recipient fish.
source: Primary MPNSTs that arose in the eye were dissected from euthanized tp53del/del animals and orthotopically transplanted into the equivalent periocular space or into the peritoneum of CG1-strain recipient fish (n = 2 primary tumors, n = 9 recipient fish total, 2 × 104 cells/fish).
evidence: This is described in the results section.

claim: All recipient animals engrafted MPNST tumor with histology similar to the primary disease.
source: All recipient animals engrafted tumor with histology similar to the primary disease (Figure 2A–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: tp53del/del angiosarcomas were successfully engrafted into CG1-recipient animals.
source: We successfully engrafted tp53del/del angiosarcomas into CG1-recipient animals and ubi:GFP+ tumor cells were easily traceable in non-fluorescent recipients (n = 3 primary tumors, n = 8 of 9 transplant fish developed tumors, Figure 2F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F-I with 8 of 9 fish engrafting.

claim: ubi:GFP+ angiosarcoma tumor cells were easily traceable in non-fluorescent recipients.
source: We successfully engrafted tp53del/del angiosarcomas into CG1-recipient animals and ubi:GFP+ tumor cells were easily traceable in non-fluorescent recipients (n = 3 primary tumors, n = 8 of 9 transplant fish developed tumors, Figure 2F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F-I with fluorescent imaging.

claim: Five of five primary leukemias engrafted into recipient fish.
source: In total, five of five primary leukemias engrafted into recipient fish with GFP+ cells disseminating widely throughout the animal by 60 days post-transplantation (n = 5 primary leukemias, n = 25 of 25 animals engrafted leukemia, Figure 2J–M, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2J-M and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP+ leukemia cells disseminated widely throughout the animal by 60 days post-transplantation.
source: In total, five of five primary leukemias engrafted into recipient fish with GFP+ cells disseminating widely throughout the animal by 60 days post-transplantation (n = 5 primary leukemias, n = 25 of 25 animals engrafted leukemia, Figure 2J–M, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2J-M with whole animal imaging.

claim: GFP+ leukemia cells invaded the recipient kidney marrow.
source: Whole animal imaging and flow cytometric analysis revealed that GFP+ cells also invaded the recipient kidney marrow, the site of hematopoiesis in adult zebrafish (Figure 2M,N).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2M,N with imaging and flow cytometry.

claim: Leukemic cells consisted of as much as 45% of the reconstituted marrow in transplanted fish.
source: Leukemic cells consisted of as much as 45% of the reconstituted marrow in transplanted fish (Figure 2N, n = 3 independent primary leukemias analyzed).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2N with flow cytometry data.

claim: The leukemic cells were large with prominent nucleoli and abundant, vacuolated cytoplasm, consistent with a rare, high-grade aggressive NK cell leukemia.
source: The leukemic cells were large with prominent nucleoli and abundant, vacuolated cytoplasm, consistent with a rare, high-grade aggressive NK cell leukemia.
evidence: This is based on cytospin and Wright/Giemsa staining shown in Figure 2O-R.

claim: In the context of gene expression profiling, tp53del/del leukemias were classified as aggressive NK cell-like leukemia.
source: In the context of gene expression profiling (outlined below), these leukemias were also similarly classified as aggressive NK cell-like leukemia, suggesting important roles for Tp53 in initiation of leukemias of NK cell origin (Figure 2Q,R).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: GFP-labeled kRASG12D-induced tp53del/del ERMS were readily transplantable when engrafted into syngeneic recipient fish.
source: Finally, GFP-labeled kRASG12D-induced tp53del/del ERMS were readily transplantable when engrafted into syngeneic recipient fish (n = 11 primary tumors analyzed, n = 47/49 fish engrafted, Figure 2S–V, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2S-V with 47/49 fish engrafting.

claim: Histology was similar between primary and transplanted MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, leukemias and ERMS.
source: Histology was similar between primary and transplanted MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, leukemias and ERMS (Figure 2B,C,E,I,M,V).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with histology images of primary and transplanted tumors.

claim: Principal component analysis identified six distinct clusters corresponding to whole CG1 syngeneic fish, leukemia, MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumor and ERMS.
source: Principal component analysis identified six distinct clusters corresponding to whole CG1 syngeneic fish, leukemia, MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumor and ERMS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with PCA plot.

claim: The upregulated leukemia gene set identified in zebrafish was significantly enriched for GO terms associated with immune system processes, leukocyte activation, immune response and lymphocyte activation.
source: For example, the upregulated leukemia gene set identified in zebrafish was significantly enriched for GO terms associated with immune system processes, leukocyte activation, immune response and lymphocyte activation.
evidence: This is based on MSigDB analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Angiosarcomas were enriched in GO gene sets associated with vasculature, blood vessel morphogenesis and cellular proliferation.
source: By contrast, angiosarcomas were enriched in GO gene sets associated with vasculature, blood vessel morphogenesis and cellular proliferation.
evidence: This is based on MSigDB analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The germ cell tumor showed enrichment of GO gene sets associated with sexual reproduction and gamete formation.
source: The germ cell tumor showed enrichment of GO gene sets associated with sexual reproduction and gamete formation.
evidence: This is based on MSigDB analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ERMS shared significant overlap of gene signatures with muscle structure, muscle contraction and muscle development.
source: As expected, ERMS shared significant overlap of gene signatures with muscle structure, muscle contraction and muscle development.
evidence: This is based on MSigDB analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Human angiosarcoma gene signature is significantly enriched in zebrafish tp53del/del angiosarcomas (FDR q-value = 0.001).
source: Using Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005), we identified significant enrichment of signatures associated with human angiosarcoma (FDR q-value = 0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), MPNST (FDR q-value = 0.00433526, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and ERMS (FDR q-value = 0, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) in the corresponding zebrafish tp53del/del tumors but not other tumor types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A with GSEA analysis.

claim: Human MPNST gene signature is significantly enriched in zebrafish tp53del/del MPNSTs (FDR q-value = 0.00433526).
source: Using Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005), we identified significant enrichment of signatures associated with human angiosarcoma (FDR q-value = 0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), MPNST (FDR q-value = 0.00433526, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and ERMS (FDR q-value = 0, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) in the corresponding zebrafish tp53del/del tumors but not other tumor types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with GSEA analysis.

claim: Human ERMS gene signature is significantly enriched in zebrafish tp53del/del ERMS (FDR q-value = 0).
source: Using Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005), we identified significant enrichment of signatures associated with human angiosarcoma (FDR q-value = 0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), MPNST (FDR q-value = 0.00433526, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and ERMS (FDR q-value = 0, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) in the corresponding zebrafish tp53del/del tumors but not other tumor types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C with GSEA analysis.

claim: tp53del/del leukemias expressed markers indicative of NK and NK-like cells.
source: Using these lineage-specific gene sets, we found that tp53del/del leukemias expressed markers indicative of NK and NK-like cells but largely failed to express genes associated with other hematopoietic cell lineages (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E with gene expression analysis.

claim: tp53del/del leukemias largely failed to express genes associated with other hematopoietic cell lineages.
source: Using these lineage-specific gene sets, we found that tp53del/del leukemias expressed markers indicative of NK and NK-like cells but largely failed to express genes associated with other hematopoietic cell lineages (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E with gene expression analysis.

claim: The top 200 most differentially regulated genes in leukemias showed significant enrichment only in NK cells (p=0.015, one-sided binomial test).
source: To independently confirm our results, we next identified the top 200 most differentially regulated genes in leukemias compared to all other tumor types and assessed if these genes were differentially expressed in each zebrafish blood lineage. Significant enrichment was only observed in NK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, p=0.015, one-sided binomial test), supporting a NK cell origin of tp53del/del leukemias.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: tp53del/del NK cell-like leukemias expressed well-known genes commonly associated with human NK cells, including il2ga and b, jak3, perforins 2,7, and 8.
source: Importantly, tp53del/del NK cell-like leukemias also expressed well-known genes commonly associated with human NK cells, including il2ga and b, jak3, perforins 2,7, and 8, and these genes were highly up-regulated when compared to all other tumor types in our analysis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with a heatmap of gene expression.

claim: Aggressive NK cell leukemias (ANKLs) have a very poor prognosis in humans.
source: In humans, aggressive NK cell leukemias (ANKLs) have a very poor prognosis and often express perforins but lack markers of mature T- and B- cell lineages (Liang and Graham, 2008; Suzuki and Nakamura, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang and Graham, 2008 and Suzuki and Nakamura, 1999.

claim: Human ANKLs often express perforins but lack markers of mature T- and B- cell lineages.
source: In humans, aggressive NK cell leukemias (ANKLs) have a very poor prognosis and often express perforins but lack markers of mature T- and B- cell lineages (Liang and Graham, 2008; Suzuki and Nakamura, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang and Graham, 2008 and Suzuki and Nakamura, 1999.

claim: In human disease, ANKLs are associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection.
source: In human disease, ANKLs are associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection, however, CD3-/CD4-/CD56+/CD13-/CD33- leukemias without EBV infection and intact germline configured T-cell receptor and immunoglobulin have been reported (Liang and Graham, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liang and Graham, 2008.

claim: Both TP53 point mutations and deletions have been identified in human ANK cell leukemias.
source: Interestingly, both TP53 point mutations and deletions have been identified in human ANK cell leukemias, suggesting a role for TP53 in pathogenesis of this disease (Soliman et al., 2014; Yagita et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soliman et al., 2014 and Yagita et al., 2000.

claim: No in vivo animal models of ANKL have been reported prior to this study.
source: Yet, to date no in vivo animal models of ANKL have been reported precluding direct functional assessment of TP53 loss in eliciting transformation of NK cells.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field that this study addresses.

claim: Significant overlap in expression exists between homozygous tp53 deletion and point-mutant MPNSTs when compared to whole fish (p=4e-321 for up-regulated genes and p=5e-182 for down-regulated genes).
source: As may be expected, we found significant overlap in expression between homozygous tp53 deletion and point-mutant MPNSTs when compared to whole fish (p=4e-321 for up-regulated genes and p=5e-182 for down-regulated genes, one-sided Fisher's exact test (Figure 3—source data 4), confirming the previously described loss-of-function activity for tp53M214K (Berghmans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing comparison with statistical analysis.

claim: The significant overlap in expression between tp53del/del and tp53M214K/M214K MPNSTs confirms the previously described loss-of-function activity for tp53M214K.
source: As may be expected, we found significant overlap in expression between homozygous tp53 deletion and point-mutant MPNSTs when compared to whole fish (p=4e-321 for up-regulated genes and p=5e-182 for down-regulated genes, one-sided Fisher's exact test (Figure 3—source data 4), confirming the previously described loss-of-function activity for tp53M214K (Berghmans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression overlap and supported by citation to Berghmans et al., 2005.

claim: Differences in gene expression were noted when comparing tp53del/del and tp53M214K/M214K MPNSTs.
source: Interestingly, differences in gene expression were also noted when comparing these tumors, likely arising from differences in the underlying mutations (Figure 3—source data 4), which are known to differentially affect Tp53 function and tumor etiology in genetically engineered mouse models.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing comparison.

claim: TP53 has roles in regulating self-renewal of normal stem cells and human cancer cells, including acute myeloid leukemia and breast cancer.
source: TP53 has roles in regulating self-renewal of normal stem cells and human cancer cells, including acute myeloid leukemia and breast cancer (Cicalese et al., 2009; Meletis et al., 2006; TeKippe et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cicalese et al., 2009; Meletis et al., 2006; TeKippe et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2010.

claim: kRASG12D-induced tumors harboring wild-type tp53 had similar frequency of tumor-propagating stem cells when compared with those of tp53del/del ERMS (p=0.647 EDLA analysis).
source: Unexpectedly, kRASG12D-induced tumors harboring wild-type tp53 had similar frequency of tumor-propagating stem cells when compared with those of tp53del/del ERMS (n ≥ 3 tumors analyzed per genotype, p=0.647 EDLA analysis, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with limiting dilution transplantation data and statistical analysis.

claim: Tp53 loss-of-function does not alter the overall frequency of tumor-sustaining, cancer stem cells in ERMS.
source: We concluded that Tp53 loss-of-function does not alter the overall frequency of tumor-sustaining, cancer stem cells in ERMS, which contrasts with previous studies that defined major roles for NOTCH1, MYF5/MYOD, and WNT signaling in regulating self-renewal and the overall number of tumor sustaining cell types in rhabdomyosarcoma (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2018; Ignatius et al., 2017; Tenente et al., 2017).
evidence: This is concluded from the limiting dilution transplantation data in Table 1.

claim: NOTCH1, MYF5/MYOD, and WNT signaling have major roles in regulating self-renewal and the overall number of tumor sustaining cell types in rhabdomyosarcoma.
source: We concluded that Tp53 loss-of-function does not alter the overall frequency of tumor-sustaining, cancer stem cells in ERMS, which contrasts with previous studies that defined major roles for NOTCH1, MYF5/MYOD, and WNT signaling in regulating self-renewal and the overall number of tumor sustaining cell types in rhabdomyosarcoma (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2018; Ignatius et al., 2017; Tenente et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2018; Ignatius et al., 2017; Tenente et al., 2017.

claim: TP53 loss is predictive of poor outcome in human ERMS.
source: TP53 loss is predictive of poor outcome in human ERMS (Seki et al., 2015); however, given that tp53 loss did not regulate the overall frequency of ERMS stem cells in zebrafish, we reasoned that loss of Tp53 might rather affect tumor invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seki et al., 2015.

claim: Only rare metastatic lesions were identified in zebrafish engrafted with tp53wt/wt ERMS (n = 5 of 58 engrafted animals).
source: Through serial imaging of engrafted fish over time, we identified only rare metastatic lesions in zebrafish engrafted with tp53wt/wt ERMS (n = 5 of 58 engrafted animals, Figure 4A–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with whole animal imaging data.

claim: tp53del/del ERMS were highly aggressive and displayed elevated local invasion and disseminated metastatic disease (n = 28 of 102 engrafted fish had metastatic ERMS, p=0.003).
source: By contrast, tp53del/del ERMS were highly aggressive and displayed elevated local invasion and disseminated metastatic disease (n = 28 of 102 engrafted fish had metastatic ERMS, p=0.003, one-sided Fisher's exact test, Figure 4I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 with whole animal imaging data and statistical analysis.

claim: Metastatic lesions in tp53del/del ERMS were confirmed on paraffin-embedded sections using both hematoxylin/eosin staining and anti-GFP antibody IHC.
source: These metastatic lesions were confirmed on paraffin-embedded sections using both hematoxylin/eosin staining and anti-GFP antibody IHC (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G,H with histology images.

claim: tp53 loss stimulates local infiltration and metastasis in ERMS.
source: Thus, our in vivo experiments demonstrate an important consequence for tp53 loss in stimulating local infiltration and metastasis, revealing a property that may account for poor outcome in RMS patients with TP53 pathway deregulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the transplantation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: tp53 loss may account for poor outcome in RMS patients with TP53 pathway deregulation.
source: Thus, our in vivo experiments demonstrate an important consequence for tp53 loss in stimulating local infiltration and metastasis, revealing a property that may account for poor outcome in RMS patients with TP53 pathway deregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing increased metastasis.

claim: Unlike available genetically engineered mouse models and human ERMS xenografts, zebrafish ERMS are metastatic.
source: This work is important, because unlike available genetically engineered mouse models and human ERMS xenografts, zebrafish ERMS are metastatic, which can be readily quantified and visualized in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the zebrafish model and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Zebrafish ERMS metastasis can be readily quantified and visualized in vivo.
source: This work is important, because unlike available genetically engineered mouse models and human ERMS xenografts, zebrafish ERMS are metastatic, which can be readily quantified and visualized in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 with serial imaging and quantification.

claim: Two pairs of TALENs were designed to target the 5' and 3' genomic sequence of tp53.
source: Four TALEN pairs (two pairs each flanking the tp53 gene locus in D. rerio) were designed to generate a ~12.1 kb deletion encompassing the entire tp53 coding sequence.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: The tp53 deletion encompasses the entire tp53 coding sequence.
source: Four TALEN pairs (two pairs each flanking the tp53 gene locus in D. rerio) were designed to generate a ~12.1 kb deletion encompassing the entire tp53 coding sequence.
evidence: This is described in the methods section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CG1 strain zebrafish are syngeneic.
source: Zebrafish used in this work included: CG1 strain zebrafish (Mizgireuv and Revskoy, 2006), CG1-strain Tg(ubi:GFP) animals that were generated using Tol2-mediated transgenesis (Kawakami et al., 2000; Mosimann et al., 2011), and rag2E450fs/E450fs;casper strain zebrafish that were used in a subset of ERMS metastasis assays.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mizgireuv and Revskoy, 2006.

source: All animal studies were approved by the Massachusetts General Hospital Subcommittee on Research Animal Care under the protocol #2011 N-000127.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.
